Product idea for India

Your appliance should tell you before it breaks.

Washing machines, fridges, air conditioners and lifts run on motors that give weeks of warning through vibration and heat. I would build the layer that listens, so a family gets a message and a booking button instead of a breakdown.

How it works, in four steps

Break it on purpose. On the maker's test rig, faults are fitted to a motor one at a time, so every reading is labelled.
Learn the fingerprint. A classifier learns what vibration and heat look like for each fault.
Ship it inside. A small model runs on a low cost chip in the appliance and decides there, so raw data stays at home. The internet is only used to send the alert.
Warn and book. The owner gets one clear message and a booking button, weeks before failure.

Try it: a simulated motor with a hidden fault.

A small health layer for everyday appliances (fridge compressor, washing machine, AC, mixer grinder, home lift, water pump). The maker already tests units on a rig and logs sensor data. That data trains a classifier. In the home, the appliance sends two cheap signals, vibration and temperature, and the app says "your washing machine bearing is wearing, book a service this month" before it fails on a wedding weekend.

Simulated motor, not real data. The model below is a five class classifier trained live in your browser on 100 simulated motor runs. Healthy motors also swing with load and room temperature, so the task is not trivial.

Where this could go

Washing machinedrum vibration, motor temperature. Bearing and unbalanced load.
Fridge and ACcompressor temperature and vibration. Failing compressor, low gas.
Mixer grindervibration and motor temperature. Worn bearing, jammed blade.
Home lift, pumpmotor temperature and vibration. Overload, dry running.
Televisionpanel and power board temperature. Failing backlight or capacitor.

The hard parts are not the model. They are fault data (units rarely fail on the rig), cheap sensors, and a service network that can act on the alert.

The business case: who pays, and why it works.

Everything in this section is a set of assumptions to test, not market data. I chose them to be believable and you can change them below. The point is to show which numbers matter.

The maker pays for the hardwareA sensor and a small chip added to each appliance. In return the maker gets fewer expensive warranty failures, a reason for owners to stay with the brand, and field data on how its products really fail.
The owner pays for peace of mindAn optional yearly plan that watches the appliance and books the fix. The first version of the product works without it, so the owner is never forced to pay.
The service partner pays per booked visitA technician network gets planned work with the right part ordered ahead, instead of emergency calls.

Value created per appliance (washing machine example)

Rupees, over the life of one appliance. Change a number and the bars move. All parties are combined here. How the value is split is a later question.

How it reaches customers

Start inside new models through one maker, because the sensor and chip are cheapest when built in. Selling to existing owners as a retrofit comes later and costs more to support.

Why now

Sensors and chips are cheap, small models can run on the chip itself without the cloud, and families already book repairs on their phones.

What owners have today

Makers' own connected apps offer some diagnostics, and booking platforms handle the repair visit. I am not aware of one product that predicts the failure and books the fix across brands. I would check this properly before relying on it.

Main risks

  • Rig faults may not match how appliances fail in homes, so field data must be collected early.
  • The share of owners who take the plan decides the owner revenue.
  • Makers take a long time to approve changes to a product.
  • False alarms make owners stop trusting the alert.

The first 30 days

Pick one appliance. Washing machine or air conditioner compressor, and one maker to approach.
Build a small rig. Test 50 motors with injected faults. Measure how many failures are caught and how many false alarms occur.
Talk to owners. Ten interviews on what they would pay and what message they would act on.
Line up service. Two repair partners agree to take booked visits, and I learn their real costs.

The right people in the right area, two hours before the work arrives.

A warehouse, factory floor or restaurant is split into areas, and the load on each area keeps changing through the day. Staff too few and queues build and throughput drops. Staff too many and paid hours sit idle. Most sites plan this by experience and a fixed roster.

The ideaUse past data to forecast the incoming work for the next two hours, in 30 minute steps. A machine learning model learns the daily pattern, the weekday effect and what the last few hours say about the next ones. Then each area's forecast is turned into the person hours it needs, using rates calibrated from history, so people can be moved before the peak arrives.
What I didDuring my summer internship at Amazon I developed this for a sort centre and optimised the process around it. The result was a 2% increase in throughput for one unit. The engine is kept separate from each site's own settings, so another site can be added without rebuilding it.
Collect. Arrivals per area and per 30 minutes, plus how fast people really work in each area.
Forecast. A model predicts the next four half hours for every area.
Convert. Forecast work divided by calibrated pace gives the person hours needed.
Act. The manager moves people before the peak, not after the queue forms.

Why it matters

ThroughputFewer bottlenecks, because capacity is in place when the volume arrives.
CostLess paid idle time, and less overtime to clear a backlog.
FairnessWorkload is spread by evidence, not by who shouts loudest.
ScaleThe same engine works at another site, a restaurant chain or a plant, with new settings.

Predictive maintenance: hear the failure before it happens.

A machine rarely breaks without warning. Vibration, temperature, pressure and efficiency drift for days or weeks first. Predictive maintenance learns what healthy looks like and what a developing fault looks like, then raises a flag early enough to act. I have built this twice, in two industries.

Rolls-Royce

Engine health classifier

Started on my own initiative. I designed a machine learning classifier that tells healthy engine data from data where a fault is developing, and built the proof of concept and then a prototype.

  • It was later added to a business jet program as an engine health monitoring function.
Ford

Vehicle health classifier

Built during a Ford sponsored data analyst fellowship. It predicts vehicle health from noisy sensor logs.

  • Over 92% accuracy on noisy logs.
  • Distinction, and the top submission in the cohort.
Label. Data from healthy and faulty machines, with the fault type known.
Describe. Turn raw signals into level, trend and spread over a short window.
Classify. A model scores each window for risk and fault type.
Decide. Set the alarm so that false alarms and missed failures are balanced by their real cost.

Try it: a failure predictor you can train and break.

This trains two machine learning models live, in your browser, on simulated machine sensor data: logistic regression and gradient boosted trees. The task is to raise an alarm on a unit before it fails, early enough to act, without crying wolf on healthy units. Change the data, the model and the cost of a miss, and watch the result move.

Honest labelling: the data is simulated by me to show the method (units with vibration, temperature, pressure and efficiency signals, load changes, hidden fault onset, and healthy units with transient spikes). It is not real engine data from Rolls-Royce or Ford.

3. What the model relies on

Permutation importance: how much the score drops when one signal is shuffled. Gain: how much each signal helped the trees split.

4. Pick the alarm threshold

An alarm fires when two checks in a row are above the threshold. Caught means the alarm came at least 5 steps before failure. An alarm on a healthy unit, or before the fault began, is a false alarm.

5. Look at one unit

Seconds decide everything. We buy soldiers more of them.

StagON is a counter drone company I co-founded with two others. We build portable, battery powered low altitude air defence for soldiers on foot and for sensitive sites. The aim in three words is detect, identify and neutralise. The first job is to see the drone early.

The problemA small drone at 120 km/h covers 1,000 m in about 30 seconds. With no early warning, the first sign is often when it is already close. That leaves only a few seconds.
What we are buildingA lightweight system that fuses several kinds of sensing to detect a drone up to 1,000 m away, confirm what it is, and give the team a clear alert early enough to take cover or act.

How early warning changes the outcome

A drone approaches from 1,100 m. Switch between a position with StagON and a position without early detection. Illustrative, and the distances follow the website timeline.

How it works, briefly

Search wide. Radio and wide view sensors watch the whole sky for anything that looks like a drone.
Cue and confirm. A second, narrow and powerful sensor is pointed at the contact to confirm what it is and track it.
Fuse. The sensors are combined into one picture. Confidence in each track fades if nothing confirms it, so the screen stays honest.
Alert. The team is told how far away it is and how long they have.
